meal feeding of rats causes an increase in liver glycogen and that the sensitivity of glycogenic enzymes to glucagon, catecholamines and metabolic stressors is reduced.
the sensitivity of glycopenolysis to glucagone, epinephrins and cyanide in the liver is influenced by the metabolic condition of the animal.

the study of the regulation of hepatic glycogenolysis by the sympathetic nervous system and the action of glucagon in the isolated perfused rat liver.
the study of the mechanisms by which the liver regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the glycogenolytic sensitivity to glucagon, as well as to epinephine and cyanide, in livers from fasted rats was higher than in the corresponding controls.
the glycogen content in livers from fed animals was not a major determinant of the sensitivity of glycogenesis.
the sensitivity of glycogenesis and glycogenolysis, as well as the glycogen content and turnover, are all affected by the metabolic condition of the liver.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sensitivity of glycogenic catabolism to epinephine, glucagon and cyanide is dependent on the glycogen content in the livers.

meal-fed rats, in contrast to the corresponding controls, are able to maintain a high glycogen content in the liver by a combination of a low sensitivity to epinephrin and a high sensitivity to glucagon.

meal-feeding, by increasing the glycogen content, increases the sensitivity of glycogenic and glycogenolytic processes to glucagon, and by decreasing the sensitivity to epinephrines, it protects glycogen stores during periods of fasting.
The main takeaway from our work is that
meal-fed rats are resistant to epinephrin-induced glycogen depletion.
the liver is not a static tissue.
